key: G major, ending in E major
intro: Heaven has a kitchen in Mahler’s Fourth: Saint Martha cooks, Peter fishes, and the saints make music. A soprano tells the story with a child’s delight, while sleigh bells and the slaughter of a lamb put a chill into the feast.

cues.title: Clarinet, horn and harp
cues.text: A clarinet opens over horn, harp and muted violas and cellos. The violins and double basses wait. Mahler marks the music Sehr behaglich — very comfortable — and warns the conductor to accompany the singer with extreme discretion.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 328: opening instrumentation, Sehr behaglich and the note to the conductor above the movement. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A child’s view of heaven
cues.text: The soprano begins with heaven’s pleasures: no earthly commotion reaches this place. Mahler asks for a childlike, cheerful voice and explicitly rules out parody. Harp and lightly plucked strings give the singer plenty of room to tell the story.
cues.evidence: Full score, opening vocal entry: Mit kindlich heiterem Ausdruck; durchaus ohne Parodie. The poem is from Des Knaben Wunderhorn; text and discussion at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bells announce a butcher
cues.text: Sleigh bells break into the song. The next verse turns to E minor and follows a lamb to slaughter: John leads it, Herod waits, and Saint Luke kills the ox. The child describes heaven’s dinner without a flicker of horror.
cues.evidence: Full score, second orchestral interlude and second vocal stanza; German text and English translation at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . E-minor second stanza: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A garden without prices
cues.text: Another burst of bells ushers in the returning first tune. Herbs and vegetables grow in heaven’s garden; fruit comes free. Deer and hares run straight into the kitchen, and Saint Martha must be the cook. The orchestra darts about with the animals.
cues.evidence: Third stanza of the Wunderhorn poem and its returning first-verse melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Full score, third vocal stanza and its quickening accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song from Hamburg
cues.text: Mahler finishes the voice-and-piano version of Das himmlische Leben in February 1892 and orchestrates it the following month. Years later he builds the Fourth Symphony around this ending. The child’s song is the oldest music in the room.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s work history dates the piano version to 10 February 1892 and the orchestral version to 12 March: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: E major after the bells
cues.text: The final sleigh-bell interruption fades. Flute and cor anglais introduce a new melody in E major above harp triplets and muted strings. The soprano waits while the orchestra discovers the quiet sound in which the symphony will end.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 349, rehearsal 12: Tempo I, Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss; flute and cor anglais, harp triplets and muted strings. Final section in E major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Music beyond the earth
cues.text: The soprano takes up the E-major tune. Heaven’s music surpasses anything on earth: eleven thousand virgins dance, and Saint Ursula laughs. The voice stays gentle over the harp’s steady triplets; there is no grand final chorus.
cues.evidence: Fourth stanza of the Wunderhorn poem, full score, printed pp. 350–353; text at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cecilia and her companions
cues.text: Cecilia and her relations become splendid court musicians. Their angelic voices bring everything to life with joy. Mahler keeps the accompaniment small: rocking harp notes, soft strings and wind phrases around the soprano’s final words.
cues.evidence: Final lines of the Wunderhorn poem: Cäcilia mit ihren Verwandten sind treffliche Hofmusikanten; full score, printed pp. 352–353.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The harp takes its time
cues.text: After the soprano finishes, cor anglais and bass clarinet fade over low strings. The harp continues alone between the held notes. Mahler writes sich Zeit lassen — take time — before the last E-major chord slips away.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 353: final instrumental bars, harp sich Zeit lassen, morendo and sustained cello and bass ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The soprano enters the small orchestra
transitions.how: The clarinet-led prelude settles into G major. The soprano begins above harp and plucked strings, with soft wind phrases around her. Mahler asks for a cheerful, childlike expression and leaves the accompaniment light enough for the words to carry.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 328–330, prelude and first vocal entry.

transitions.title: Bells disturb the G-major refrain
transitions.to: B · Bells before the butcher’s verse
transitions.how: The first verse closes like a quiet hymn over muted strings and horns. Sleigh bells and high winds interrupt, with strings striking col legno. The soprano then begins a new melody in E minor for the verse about the lamb’s slaughter.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first refrain, sleigh-bell interlude and second verse; movement guide and text: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The first song returns after bells
transitions.from: B · Bells before the butcher’s verse
transitions.to: A′ · Bells, then the garden’s abundance
transitions.how: The second verse’s hymn-like close gives way to another sleigh-bell interruption. The soprano recovers the first verse’s melody for the garden stanza, with winds and strings returning to its lighter accompaniment. Faster figures soon animate the running animals and swimming fish.
transitions.evidence: Full score, second refrain, orchestral interlude and third verse; https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The last rattle of sleigh bells
transitions.from: A′ · Bells, then the garden’s abundance
transitions.how: The verse about Saint Martha ends in a broad refrain. Sleigh bells, triangle, winds and strings break in once more. This interlude quickly dwindles, clearing the orchestra for a new key and a softer tune.
transitions.evidence: Full score, third refrain and final bell interlude before rehearsal 12.

transitions.title: Flute and cor anglais find E major
transitions.to: C · Flute and cor anglais in E major
transitions.how: The bells and forceful wind figures die away. E major settles over a harp accompaniment in triplets, and flute and cor anglais begin the last tune. Muted strings join beneath a direction to remain very tender and mysterious to the end.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 349, rehearsal 12: Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss.

transitions.title: The singer takes the E-major tune
transitions.from: C · Flute and cor anglais in E major
transitions.how: The soprano enters the E-major music already established by the winds. Harp triplets continue beneath muted strings and soft wind chords. The orchestral melody becomes the song of heaven’s musicians without another bell interruption.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 349–351, orchestral introduction and fourth vocal stanza.

transitions.title: Low winds answer the last words
transitions.to: Coda · The harp outlasts the voice
transitions.how: The soprano finishes over E-major harmony. Cor anglais and bass clarinet continue the line, then fade with the horns. Harp notes slow above sustained cellos and basses; the score asks the harpist to take time before the final chord.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 353: instrumental postlude and harp direction sich Zeit lassen.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, IV. Das himmlische Leben, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Fourth movement, printed pp. 328–353, rehearsal figures 1–15: four vocal stanzas, sleigh-bell interludes and the E-major ending.

timeline.note: A clarinet and a horn with harp, over muted violas and cellos; violins and basses rest.
Oboes, cor anglais, bass clarinet and bassoons add soft phrases; the basses pluck.
The soprano sings over clarinets, harp and discreet pizzicato strings.
Flutes and clarinets quicken with the voice as the text turns to dancing and singing.
Muted strings and soft horns support the hymn-like close of the verse about Saint Peter.
Sleigh bells, triangle and bells-up woodwinds rattle in the minor; strings strike with the wood of the bow.
The soprano sings the lamb’s verse to a new melody, with oboe and bass clarinet answering.
The first melody returns for the garden’s herbs and fruit.
The tempo quickens: swirling strings and woodwinds, with brief sleigh bells, for running game and darting fish.
The refrain swells for Saint Martha the cook, then ebbs.
Sleigh bells and triangle ring with fortissimo winds and strings, then fade to pp.
Flute and cor anglais introduce the E-major tune over harp triplets and muted strings.
The soprano takes the new tune over muted strings, harp triplets and soft winds.
Harp triplets rock beneath muted strings and the voice.
Cor anglais and bass clarinet fade; the harp takes its time; cellos and basses sustain softly.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
